newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: W-A CRISIS TALKS FAIL TO AVERT INDUSTRIAL ACTION TODAY

Unions are warning they'll continue their industrial campaign in Western Australia, despite the ACTU and the state government admitting some progress was made during crisis talks last night. The talks began during a 24 hour stop-work across the state which affected airports, public services, transport and health services.
ACTU president Jennie George met with Premier Richard Court for two-and-a-half hours to outline the union movement's objections to the Government's new industrial reforms.
Premier Court says the government is always prepared to negotiate on the detail of the legislation, while Ms George says things are looking better than they did a week ago.
The talks weren't enough however, to avert power cuts today due to union action.
PHONE LINK TO DECIDE NEW LIBERAL DIRECTOR
The Federal Liberal Party executive will hold a telephone hook-up today to decide on a replacement Federal Director.
Current Director, Andrew Robb, announced his resignation last week.
Mr Robb has spent seven years in the job, and a total of nearly ten years in the Party organisation.
RETIREMENT SAVINGS A/C'S SET TO GO AHEAD
The Federal Government's planned Retirement Savings Accounts are set to proceed with the Senate poised to finally approve one of the Coalition's key election committments.
The Senate last month rejected legislation setting up the Accounts, with the Democrats claiming the planned alternative to superannuation would have benefitted employers rather than workers.
After weeks of negotiations the Government has reached a compromise position with the Democrats that'll see the bill pass the Senate when Parliament resumes next week.
It's understood the Government has accepted some of the Democrats' arguements and changed the legislation accordingly.
The Retirement Savings Accounts will be offered by banks and a range of other financial institutions from July.
CAPSICUM SPRAYS FOR TASSIE COPS
Tasmania's police hope to have capsicum sprays available for general issue to officers within 12 months.
The Police Association has been pushing for the introduction of the sprays to defuse potentially violent incidents rather than relying on the threat of guns.
The Association's secretary Des LeFevre says the acceptance of the sprays in Victoria shows they can be a valuable aid.
Mr LeFevre says there is some concern that there's been no response to calls for the public sale of capsicum spray to be banned.
NORFOLK ISLAND GOES TO THE POLLS
Australia's prospect as a Rupublic, and tourism are two of the main issues facing voters at today's Norfolk Island elections.
A new Parliament will be voted in on the Island north east of Sydney, which is home to about 18-hundred people, and Australia's only self-governming external territory.
The Island's Chief Minister, Mike King, says the main election issue is the future of the island's tourism industry, following Ansett's decision to stop flying to the Island.
He also says many Norfolk Islanders are fiercely loyal to the British crown, and feel the republican issue should be addressed during the life of the next Parliament.
